intro: Rachmaninoff plays his most persistent encore for Victor in 1921. Three low notes grow into chords so broad that the score needs four staves to hold them.

sections.label: B · Triplets gather force
sections.mNote: The Agitato melody climbs over running notes

sections.label: C · Bell chords return
sections.mNote: The opening spreads across four staves

sections.label: D · Quiet chords over C♯
sections.mNote: A low C♯ holds beneath the closing chords

cues.title: Three low notes
cues.text: A–G♯–C♯: three notes struck in octaves, fortissimo. The answer is astonishingly quiet, marked ppp. The same three-note descent keeps tolling beneath the chords.
cues.evidence: Bosworth (1896) and Universal Edition (1910), opening upbeat and bars 1–4; Petro Kostandy’s Mutopia engraving. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Triplets around a falling tune
cues.text: The Agitato sets triplets whirling around a melody that descends E–D♯–D♮–C♯. The right hand has two jobs: its outer notes sing while the fingers underneath keep moving.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 14–17: Agitato, with the descending melody separately stemmed above triplet quavers. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The encore that follows him
cues.text: Rachmaninoff writes the Prelude at nineteen. Years later, audiences still demand it before they let him leave the platform. The short piano piece follows its composer into recital halls around the world.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker, notes to Hyperion CDA66081, on the Prelude’s composition and persistent demand as an encore. The issued take of this 1921 Victor transfer remains unidentified. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6690_66081

cues.title: Four staves, two hands
cues.text: The opening chords return at Tempo primo, now marked fff pesante — very loud and heavy. Rachmaninoff writes on four staves, two for each hand. The little bell figure fills the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 45–48: Tempo primo, fff pesante and four-stave piano notation. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: C♯ under the last chords
cues.text: A low C♯ stays beneath the last sequence of chords. The hands move by small steps above it, and the final C♯ minor chord is held under a fermata, ppp.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 55–61: sustained low C♯ and the final ppp chord with fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
